headline: Arithmetic as Geometry: A Mathematician's Oldest Secret
lede: A single tweet — "Everything is geometry. Addition is geometry. Bodmas is geometry" — captures the jolt of a specific mathematical epiphany: that the rules drilled into schoolchildren are not arbitrary but the shadow of something spatial and ancient. The insight is real, and it runs deeper than it first sounds.
body:
The ancient Greeks had no algebra in the modern sense. For Euclid and his predecessors, all mathematics was geometry. When they proved that the area of the square on a triangle's hypotenuse equals the combined areas of the squares on the other two sides, they meant *literal* squares drawn on paper — not symbolic *a² + b² = c²*. Numbers themselves were understood as lengths. What we call arithmetic was, for them, the manipulation of line segments and areas.

The number line makes this concrete. **Addition** is geometric translation: move three units to the right, then four more, and you land at seven. Subtraction reverses the direction. Multiplication scales a length — stretching or compressing it by a factor. These are not analogies layered on top of arithmetic; they are the structure from which arithmetic inherits its coherence.

*BODMAS* (Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction) — the mnemonic for order of operations — also makes geometric sense once you see multiplication as scaling and addition as translation. Scaling and then translating gives a different result than translating and then scaling, which is why the order of operations is not arbitrary. It preserves the geometric consistency of the system.

The formal unification came with René Descartes in the 17th century. *Coordinate geometry* — the Cartesian plane taught in every secondary school — proved that any algebraic equation can be read as a curve in space, and any curve described as an equation. Algebra and geometry turned out to be two languages for one underlying reality, a duality that would later animate everything from calculus to modern physics.

The feeling of revelation @parmita describes is well documented among people who encounter mathematics taught visually rather than procedurally. Channels like 3Blue1Brown have made this their entire project — animating the geometric bones beneath formulas that most students only ever see as strings of symbols. The epiphany is genuine; the geometry was always there.

concepts.definition: A straight line on which every point corresponds to a real number, with positive numbers to the right and negative to the left. It makes arithmetic operations visually concrete: addition is rightward movement, subtraction leftward, and so on. The number line is the simplest one-dimensional geometric space.

A rule specifying the sequence in which arithmetic operations must be performed: Brackets first, then Orders (exponents), then Division and Multiplication (left to right), then Addition and Subtraction (left to right). Known as PEMDAS in American usage. The rule exists because multiplication and addition do not commute with each other in the same way — applying them in the wrong order yields different results.

The system, formalized by Descartes, that places geometric figures on a numbered grid (the Cartesian plane) so that every curve or shape can be expressed as an algebraic equation and vice versa. It is the bridge that made algebra and geometry formally equivalent rather than merely analogous.

The practice of reading algebraic operations as spatial transformations — addition as translation, multiplication as scaling or rotation, exponentiation as repeated scaling. This view predates symbolic algebra: the ancient Greeks reasoned about what we call multiplication entirely through the geometry of rectangles and areas.
